h.strategy: Naive reasoning predicts substitution: if something similar exists elsewhere, an edit helps less. Experts find this obvious, so at most two hypotheses may use it. At least three hypotheses must predict the opposite, complementarity, where an edit helps MORE because a different kind of component elsewhere supplies what it lacks. At least two must predict a reversal, where a usually beneficial edit becomes harmful under a specific condition through trainability, merged-signal scale, or over-capacity. Never condition on the edited field's own value or on settings that make the edit inert. Each hypothesis must couple two different fields, and no condition setting may appear more than twice. In each 'why', give the mechanism in two or three sentences, state why an expert might bet the other way, and name the refuting comparison. The critic should replace any hypothesis that duplicates another's mechanism.

hyps.why: An identity path already reaching the output makes an extra conv3x3 on 2->3 less valuable.
With an identity route to node 3 already present, a 1x1 conv from node 1 adds little.
If edge 5 is none, node 2 is a dead end so a conv on 1->2 cannot contribute.
If 2->3 is removed, features computed into node 2 never reach the output, so the conv is wasted.
With edge 0 removed node 1 gets no input, so a skip on 1->2 forwards nothing.
Node 2 already receives a conv3x3 from the chain, so a second conv3x3 from the input is partly redundant.
Node 3 already gets a conv3x3 from node 1, so a second conv3x3 from node 2 is largely redundant.
Replacing a removed edge 0 with a conv3x3 restores the whole 1-node path and gains far more than replacing a pool or skip.
Adding a conv3x3 where the direct input-to-output edge was absent yields a larger gain than upgrading an existing op.
Two parallel direct conv3x3 routes into the output are substitutes, so the second adds less.
